description_full: Tompkins Financial Corporation, a financial holding company, provides commercial and consumer banking, leasing, trust and investment management, financial planning and wealth management, and insurance services. It operates through two segments: Banking, and Wealth Management. The company accepts various deposit products, including checking and savings accounts, time deposits, and IRA products. It also offers loans for various business purposes, including real estate financing, construction, equipment financing, accounts receivable financing, and commercial leasing; residential mortgage loans; personal loans; home equity loans; residential real estate loans; commercial and industrial loans; commercial real estate loans; agriculture loans; and consumer and other loans, such as direct and indirect personal installment loans, automobile financing, and overdraft lines of credit. In addition, the company provides letters of credit and sweep accounts; credit and debit cards; deposit and cash management, internet-based account, remote deposit, safe deposit, ATM, voice response, and mobile and internet banking services; trust and estate; financial and tax planning services; property and casualty, life, disability, and long-term care insurance services; employee benefit consulting services; and insurance planning services. It primarily serves individuals, corporate executives, small business owners, and high net worth individuals. Tompkins Financial Corporation was founded in 1836 and is headquartered in Ithaca, New York.

financial_summary: Tompkins Financial Corporation is a small-cap financial services business with a $1.4B market cap on $447M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +13% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 14% against a 8% cost of capital, a 6-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $32M in free cash flow — roughly 7 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders. Cash conversion is thin at 0.24×, however, which raises the oldest question in analysis: are these earnings backed by cash?.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 1.7× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 2.6% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 6.5% of the shares, and within its sector the business captures 1.9× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 50% operating margin runs 21pp above the Financial Services median (29%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.94x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+5.7% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.02 across 512 companies in the universe; the top four hold 20% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 51% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 5% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 26% and a beta of 0.70, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.12 vs 5y 0.62), so read it loosely.
About $10.1M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 39% in the 2020 crash, 19% in the 2022 bear market and 45% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $91.40 (margin of safety -9%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 31%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $67.43 to $128 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Financial Services peers: cheaper on P/E 7.9 vs 12.2, richer on P/FCF 44.7 vs 12.9 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 29% below its 10-year median.
The 2 covering analysts target $106 on average, 6% above the price.
The price implies 5.5% annual cash-flow growth.
prof: ROIC of 14% earns above the cost of capital of 8.3%, but the 6pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.33).
It converts 7% of revenue into free cash flow.
It earns a 17% return on equity.
Operating margin is running 17pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 13.2% over 3 years, 8.3% over 5 years and 6.4% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 18%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 6.6% on average.
Analysts expect 4.3% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own 6.5%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 72%.
It returns 2.6% a year to shareholders (0.1% in buybacks and 3.0% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 36 consecutive years, raising it 2.9% a year over the last five.
people: With about 813 employees, each generates about $549K of revenue, in line with the Financial Services median, and productivity has risen 7.6% a year.
That works out to $39K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.7M (3x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
